decay width of the SM gauge bosons is taken from the input model files.



B.1. Mathematica Code 139

• All relevant decay processes for the computation of the total width are stored in fout-

listDecays. Here, we save the FA particle identifier in each column, with the first
column denoting the decaying particle and the other two the final-state particles.

• We identify the type of the participating particles in the decay with the function de-

terminType[sts_,ind_]. The inputs are any row of the list foutDecayslist sts_

and the corresponding column number int_.

• The generated squared amplitudes for the decays and their decay widths are stored in
the lists finalDecays and finalDecaysWidth, respectively.

The last block is the Mathematica to C++ conversion part. Here, the previously obtained
expressions for the (co-)annihilation amplitudes squared, the partial decay widths and the
relevant informations of the models are converted into C++ files. This block consists of the
following functions and lists

• The list inifunc[i] is used to store for each unique channel that contributes to the
computation of the relic abundance, the processname, the mass, the FA identifier, and
the tokenized amplitudes squared. The input parameter i is an integer and goes from
1 to the total number of different initial states.

• external and internal are lists that store all external and internal variables of the
model and their definitions, respectively.

• The list neutraldsmasses stores all the masses of the neutral dark sector particles.

• processnameDecays and possibleiniDecays are auxiliary lists that store the names
of the decay processes and the corresponding decaying particles, respectively.

• inifuncDecays[i] is analogous to inifunc[i] but is used for decay processes. In addi-
tion, it contains two extra columns corresponding to the couplings and particleType

lists.

• runMasses contains the masses of the strange, charm, bottom, and top quarks.

• model.hpp, model.cpp, init.cpp, parametermap.cpp, loadparameters.cpp, and load-
tokens.cpp contain the declarations and initialization routines for all external and in-
ternal model parameters, tokens, amplitudes squared, partial and total decay widths,
dark-sector masses, and the masses and widths of the relevant s-channel propagators.
The file model.hpp is located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/, while all remaining files
are stored in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/. If external parameters depend on
the running quark masses contained in runMasses, they must be redefined in loadpa-

rameters.cpp such that their values are updated whenever the renormalization scale
of the running masses changes. The only exception is the top quark, for which the
user-defined pole mass is used.

• calcwidths.cpp contains the routines for computing the running quark masses at a
given energy scale as well as the total widths of the relevant s-channel mediators. For
decay processes, the running masses are evaluated at a scale equal to the pole mass of
the decaying particle, whereas for DM (co-)annihilation processes, the scale is chosen
as twice the DM mass.

• all[possibleini].cpp contains the expressions for the amplitudes squared of all DM
(co-)annihilation channels associated with a given initial state [possibleini]. These
files are located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s, with separate files for
different initial states.



140 B RelExt - Overview on the Mathematica Code and Direct Detection Class

• [possibleini]flux.cpp contains the amplitudes squared multiplied by the correspond-
ing flux factors, where the latter are defined in $RelExt/sources/utils.cpp. An
additional multiplicative factor, symfac, may be included to account for equivalent pro-
cesses removed by the removeDuplicate[] routine. These files are stored in $RelEx-

t/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s.

• totalW[possibleini]Decays.cpp contains the expressions for the partial decay widths
of the relevant s-channel mediators, where [possibleini]Decays denotes the decaying
particle. The files are located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s, with one
file per mediator. For scalar and pseudoscalar particles, hard-coded partial_width

functions are employed. These functions take as input the particle types in the final
state, their masses, and the couplings extracted from the amplitudes squared, as de-
scribed in Sec. 10.1. For all other particle types, the decay widths are computed using
FeynCalc. Off-shell decay channels are assigned a width of zero.

• prtcls.cpp contains the definitions of all particle and anti-particle names used in the
model. Particles that are their own anti-particles are listed only once.

Abstract

In this work, we review 3-dimensional gravity by canonically analyzing the Hilbert-

Palatini action. We apply a time gauge used in 4-dimensional loop quantum grav-

ity [14] to the simpler case of the 3-dimensional loop quantum gravity. By time

gauge fixing this Hilbert-Palatini action it leads to the Gauss constraints, the spa-

tial diffeomorphism constraints, the Hamiltonian constraint and a new constraint

C. The gauge symmetries generated by this new constraints are spacetime diffeo-

morphism and SO(2) gauge transformations. We solve the dynamics of the theory

by providing a regularization of the generalized projector operator in terms of the

Hamiltonian constraint. We provide the definition of the physical scalar product

which can be represented in terms of a sum over finite spinfoam amplitudes. Then

we establish a clear-cut link between the canonical quantization of the new theory

to the spinfoam model (Ponzano-Regge model) defined in terms of the SU(2) spin

networks.

Chapter 1

Introduction and Motivation

1.1 Quantum Gravity

The task of quantizing gravity is one of the outstanding problems of modern

theoretical physics. Attempts to reconcile quantum theory and general relativity

(GR) date back to the early part of the twentieth century. Several decades of

hard work have yielded an abundance of insights into quantum field theory. But

despite this enormous effort, no one has yet succeeded in formulating a complete,

self-consistent quantum theory of gravity [5].

Einstein’s description of gravity as a curvature of spacetime (geometry of curved

spacetime) was seen as a game changer at the time, as this idea totally moved away

from the notion of gravity as a force. The consequence of this was the formulation

of the theory of GR which gave a deep insight into the geometric structure of the

universe at the macroscopic level.

Quantum mechanics (QM), which describes the microscopic world was formulated

based on the laws of probability. It allows for a discrete energy spectrum instead of

a continuous radiation. QM uses the time evolution of quantum states described by

the Schrodinger equation in which the Hamiltonian generates the time evolution.

This means that physical quantities can change only in discrete amounts and not

in a continuous way [27].

Our understanding of physics, and in general nature have been greatly influenced

by QM and GR. Both principles have revolutionized the pivotal structures of New-

tonian physics. The notion of absolute time and space ceases to exist, but rather

space and time and distances between points of the spacetime manifold, that is,

the metric themselves become dynamical objects [27, 28]. Further, the determin-

istic nature of Newton’s equations of motion evaporates at a fundamental level,

1

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



rather dynamics is reigned by probabilities underlying the Heisenberg uncertainty

principle.

A usual phenomenon in fundamental physics is to reconcile two different concep-

tual theories to find a new synthesis, a satisfactory physical theory must therefore

combine both of these fundamental principles, QM and GR, in a consistent way

and which will be called quantum gravity (QG). However, despite the success sto-

ries of both QM and GR, the quantization of the gravitational field has turned

out to be one of the most challenging unsolved problems in theoretical and math-

ematical physics.

The reason for this incompatibility is that, GR requires spacetime to be a dy-

namical field, describing the notion of force as a geometry and also requires an

independent background structure. On the other hand, QM requires a dynamical

field to be quantized, and in addition requires a non-dynamical background space-

time (Hilbert space) for it to take place. In GR, spacetime is dynamical, while

in QM, any dynamical entity is made up of quanta and can be in probabilistic

superposition states.

Not only are there conceptual differences in quantizing gravity, there are techni-

cal obstacles also facing the new synthesis. Einstein’s equations which governs

the theory of gravity are highly non-linear, and hence very difficult to solve. In

addition, conventional field quantization methods which are based on the weak-

field perturbation expansion fail in their application to GR since they yield a

non-renormalizable theory. GR, hence must be replaced by a more fundamental

description that appropriately includes the quantum degrees of freedom of gravity

[24].

However, it is clear that while GR has given a very consistent framework for doing

classical physics, it has not yet been successful in bringing the quantum realm

in its wake [21]. Attempts have been made for decades to formulate a consistent

theory of quantum gravity, but with no success so far.

1.2 Loop Quantum Gravity

The past decades have seen an increase in active research in the field of quantum

theory of gravity, with some claiming to have found a quantum theory of gravity.

Notably among them is string theory, which is based on the physical hypothesis

that elementary objects are extended rather than particle-like [27]. A very rich

unified theory which includes Yang-Mills fields and gravitons, and free of ultravio-

let divergences are a few of string theory’s successful story. However, this comes at

a cost of additional physics such as supersymmetry, extra dimensions, an infinite

number of fields with an arbitrary masses and spins.

In light of this another active area of research in QG is Loop Quantum Gravity

(LQG) which takes a different approach to string theory. LQG is a canonical

and background independent base approach to the quantization of gravity paying

special attention to the conceptual lessons of GR [9, 23, 27, 28]. It proposes that

spacetime is actually divided into small chucks, when you zoom out it appears

to be a smooth sheet, but when you zoom in, it is a bunch of dots connected by

lines or loops. These small fibres, which are woven together offer an explanation

of gravity.

LQG is based on a Hamiltonian formulation of GR at the classical level. In this

formulation, spacetime is foliated into a family of hypersurfaces of constant time

with coordinates on each slice. LQG is a straightforward quantization procedure

of GR with the physical inputs of the theory been the well-tested physical theories

of QM and GR, there are no major additional physical hypothesis or assumption

made in the construction of the theory [27]. All it tries to do is to merge the

conceptual ideas of GR into QM. In addition, LQG is based on assumption that

even if Einstein’s equations are modified at high energy, the general-relativistic

notion of space and time are assumed to be true.

The theory is formulated in the more physical four dimensional case. It was

initially formulated in terms of the metric variables which was due to Arnowitt,

Deser and Misner [28], hence the name ADM formulation. In this formulation, the

In carrying out canonical quantization, the guiding principle is mostly that of

Dirac. The first is to find a representation of the phase space variables as operators,

acting on some kinematical Hilbert space Hkin. This representation of the phase

space variables should map Poisson brackets into commutators. Next is to define

the constraints into self-adjoint operators in Hkin, and finally the solutions of

these constraints are characterize to define an inner product leading to a physical

Hilbert space Hphy.

The Poisson bracket between the Ashtekar-Barbero connection and the densitized

triad resulted in a delta function (distribution), this leads to a not well-defined

function. A regularization of the Poisson bracket is needed to address this problem,

and this is done by smearing the phase space variables to obtain the holonomy-flux

algebra. The regularization open up ways to quantize these constraints, and such

they (constraints) become operators on a kinematical Hilbert space. For more

on loop quantum gravity the reader is advice to read [23, 27, 28] and references

therein.

1.3 Loops and Spin Networks

The choice of different algebra of basic field functions to promote to quantum

operators makes LQG stands out among other different quantization techniques.

That choice is a non-canonical algebra based on the holonomies of the gravitational

connection [23, 27].

The holonomy in LQG becomes a quantum operator creating ”loop states”1. In a

background independent theory like LQG, the position of a loop state is relevant

only with respect to other loops, and not with respect to the background [27].

The space spanned by these loop states are not too singular nor too many, thereby

providing a basis for the Hilbert space of LQG. A finite linear combination of some

of these loop states form a well defined orthonormal basis in the Hilbert space of

a lattice Yang-Mills theory. These orthonormal basis are the spin networks states

which eventually form the basis of the mathematical structure of LQG.

As stated earlier, one will like to know what the quanta of space (quantum prop-

erties of space) are, and how to describe them, in the pursuit of a quantum theory

of spacetime. Interactions of physical systems with other systems may occur in

”quanta” and these quanta are determined by the spectral properties of the op-

erators representing the quantities involved in the interaction with the systems.

The interactions with the gravitational field (spacetime) are through geometric

structures of the physical space resulting in measurements of length, area and

volume.

The spectrum of both volume and area turns out to be discrete. From the spectral

of the volume, the quanta of space can be thought of as grains of space. These

grains of space lie adjacent to each, where in this case adjacency means being

contiguous, or being in touch, or being nearby. If one consider a quantum state

of space formed by P grains of space, where some are in contact with one another

[27].

Then representing this state as an abstract graph Γ with P nodes: these nodes of

the graph represent the grains of the space; the links of the graph connect adjacent

grains and represent the surfaces separating two adjacent grains. The quantum

state is then characterized by the graph Γ, with the labels on the nodes and on

the links, and a graph with these labels is called a spin network.

LQG has been able to predict the discretness of the spectrum of geometrical op-

erators like area and volume. The formulation of LQG in terms of the Ashtekar-

1.4 Motivation and Goal of Thesis

General relativity in three dimensions is said to be ”simple” but not trivial mak-

ing it an interesting, and as such a large area of research providing an insight

into quantum gravity for the more physical four dimension. Physically three di-

mensional gravity is a topological field theory, meaning it has no degrees of [5]

freedom2 and its manifold is regarded as a two surface with time.

Conceptually both (2 + 1)-dimensional gravity and (3 + 1)-dimensional gravity

are equivalent and many of the fundamental issues carry over to quantum gravity

at the lower dimensional setting. Although (2+1)-dimensional model is much

simpler, mathematically and physically, and we can write down a quantum theory

for the model.

There are however few instances were (2+1)-dimensional solutions are quite dif-

ferent physically from those of (3+1)-dimensional, and in addition the (2+1)-

dimensional model does not help in understanding the dynamics of quantum grav-

ity. Based on the analysis of conceptual problems such as nature of time, the role

of topology and topology change, the relationship among different approaches to

quantization, the model has really proven highly instructive [5].

Canonical analysis of (2+1)-dimensional gravity [3] result in the flatness and Gauss

constraints, defining a normal to the hypersurface x0 =const, the Hamiltonian and

spatial diffeomorphism constraints are derived. These constraints generate equal

time hypersurface which can be deformed and pushed forward in various ways. A

geometric algebra reflected in the Poisson algebra of the constraints- known as the

Dirac’s hypersurface deformation algebra3 is satisfied by these deformations of the

hypersurface. However a quantum representation of this algebra (see [3] and other

references therein for more details) has not been reached yet even in the simple

case of three dimensional gravity.

Since three dimensional gravity is simple, one will like to explore if it is possible

gauge theory, and as such performing a time gauge fixing in three dimensional

Description of a quantum space is an issue in quantum gravity, in (3+1)-dimensional

LQG and as well in (2 + 1)-dimensional LQG. The quantum space in both cases

are describe in terms of SU(2) spin networks, the question then is, if the 2+1 time

Addressing some of the questions raised above, and also understanding the physics

that can be studied as a result of the time gauge fixing in (2+1)-dimensional LQG.

In addition, how does the time gauge contribute meaningfully in understanding

loop quantum gravity, in general motivated this research.

1.5 Organization of Work

We have tried to make this work self-contained and to present all materials needed

for understanding the foundations and the theoretical framework of loop quantum

gravity and in particular the notion of time gauge fixing in (2 + 1)-dimensional

loop quantum gravity. Furthermore, we have tried to understand the dynamics of

the time gauge action in canonical quantization.

In chapter 2 we discuss the canonical formulation of 3d gravity. We begin with a

2.1 General Theory on Canonical Formalism

A dynamical system in classical mechanics consists of a phase space1Γ which is

a Poisson (usually symplectic) manifold and a function Hcl : Γ −→ R called

the (classical) Hamiltonian of energy function. For example, for a single particle

moving along a real line, Γ is the cotangent bundle T (R)∗.

In quantum machanics, the phase space Γ is replaced by the set of rays in a

complex Hilbert space H, and the space F(Γ) of functions on Γ by the algebra

Op(H) of (not necessarily bounded) operators on H. For example, in the case of

a single particle moving along the real line, H is the space of square-integrable

functions of x ∈ R.

In section 1.4, three dimensional gravity was discussed as a topological theory

with no local degrees of freedom. This feature makes the description of spacetime

as a collection of patches (contractible open set of spacetime manifold), solutions

of the Einstein equations are isometric to a model spacetime which is determined

by the signature and the sign (or vanishing) of the cosmological constant.

For example, in Lorentzian signature with vanishing cosmological constant, the

model spacetime is Minkowski space while in the Euclidean signature and positive

cosmological constant it is the three-sphere, and so on [5]. This picture leads to

the description of (2 + 1)-dimensional gravity in terms of “geometric structures.”

Depending on the topology of the manifoldM, these local solutions may be glued

together to obtain non-trivial global solutions of the Einstein equations. This

is mathematically executed by the isometry group of the local model spacetime

(the 3d Poincare group ISO(2, 1) or the orthogonal group SO(4) in the examples

mentioned above). These groups are the local isometries of the model spacetime.

Matter in the form of point particles can be described geometrically in terms

of defects of the model spacetime. The space of all these geometric structures,

suitably defined, constitutes the phase space of 3d gravity. In addition, the phase

space provides us with a symplectic form (Poisson brackets) which is needed for

canonical quantization.

Canonical formulation plays a big role in the quantization of gravity. In chapter 1,

we discussed about quantum gravity precisely loop quantum gravity and the chal-

lenges in quantizing gravity. Some of the conceptual challenges like the meaning

2.5 Algebra of Constraints

The appearance of constraints, which generate gauge symmetries, is, as one can

expert, a general feature of systems with gauge symmetries. The group structure

of gauge transformations is reflected in the algebra of constraints, in particular

by the fact that the Poisson brackets between constraints is again a combination

of constraints. If this is the case for a given set of constraints, it will be called

first class [10]. However not all constraints are related by gauge symmetries, in

particular there are second class constraints, for which the Poisson brackets do

not vanish on the constraint hypersurface. In what follows, we try to examine if

the constraints (2.40) are first class constraints, and of particular interest to us

of these Poisson bracket algebras, are whether if they completely determine the

theory.

The choice of a basic set of phase space function {f} is an integral part of canonical

quantization. This set is promoted into operators {f̂} on some kinematical Hilbert

space. By promoting the set into operators, they should map Poisson brackets into

commutators, i.e

[f̂ , ĝ] = i~{f̂, g}. (3.1)

However, this basic set should be sufficiently large, so as to distinguish between

phase space points.

The result of the Poisson bracket between the diad and the spin connection at

the classical level gives a dirac delta function. At the quantum level, this delta

function has no equivalent proper operators. Hence one must smear the canonical

variables with an appropriate smooth and fast decaying function, in order to select

a proper set of the basic variables at the quantum level.

In selecting a proper set of the basic variable, the Poisson bracket between them

should result in a simple expression forming an algebra. By forming an algebra,

quantization of this basic set become feasible. Furthermore, one would like that the

phase space functions transform in a simple way under gauge transformations, so

that these can be implemented as gauge transformations in a kinematical Hilbert

space.

Subsequent discussions in this chapter will focus on the descretized form of the

spin connection and the diad, these form a basic set of the phase space function

to be quantized. Computation of the Poisson bracket between these basic set will

be carried out. The result will show a much simpler expression compared to the

Chapter 5

Dynamics

The spinfoam approach of quantum gravity aims at constructing a rigorous well

defined mathematical notion of path integral for LQG as a tool for solving the

dynamics of the theory [19]. Characterization of the kernel of the quantum con-

straints of the theory given by quantization of the classical constraints of general

relativity defines the dynamics. The aim of these spinfoam models is to explicitly

construct a generalized projection operator from Hkin into the kernel of quantum

scalar constraint.

In [19], the authors establish a clear cut link between the spin foam approach and

the canonical quantization of three dimensional gravity. This they achieved by

constructing a physical scalar product (matrix element) of a regularized projector

operator which can be represented in terms of sum of finite spin foam amplitudes.

In this present work, we make a link between these approaches (i.e. spin foam and

canonical quantization), and to understand how the time gauge procedure from

SU(2) to SO(2) works at the quantum level. Essentially, we want to solve the

dynamics of our theory, by first constructing the matrix element of the projector

P on the physical Hilbert space.

In chapter 4, a kinematical Hilbert space of the theory in terms of the holonomies

was defined. And this can be seen as a first step towards understanding the

quantum geometry [17] of spin foams and its link to canonical formalism. In the

long run, the goal is to have a spin foam approach whose boundary states have an

SO(2) invariant spin networks.

Chapter 6

Conclusion and Outlook

In this thesis, we time gauge fix the three dimensional Hilbert-Palatini action and

got some new physics resulting from the canonical analysis.

The triad is decomposed into its various components via the time gauge (2.27). In

addition, we applied the triad decomposition to carry out a canonical analysis on

the Hilbert-Palatini action. The diad and the spin connection (two dimensions)

emerge as the new dynamical variables of the new theory.

By time gauge fixing the Hilbert-Palatini action, the usual constraints associated

to an action upon a canonical analysis is carried are obtain, thus the Gauss,

the spatial diffeomorphism and the Hamiltonian constraints. However, a new

constraint, i.e., C also emerges. In computing the time evolution associated with

the Gauss constraint G, the new theory generates an internal rotation in two

dimensions. Additionally, diffeomorphism invariance is achieved from the time

evolution associated with the spatial diffeomorphism constraint V .

In computing the algebra of constraints for the constraints of the new theory,

we found out the new theory was consistent and closed, in the sense that all

the Poisson brackets between the different constraints vanish on the constraint

hypersurface. The gauge transformation of the new system is an SO(2) gauge

transformation.

In chapter 3, a descretized form of the new dynamical variables is defined. These

form a basic set of the phase space function to be quantized. The Poisson bracket

between these basic set result in a much simpler expression compared to the non-

descretized will be carried out. The result shows a much simpler expression com-

pared to the non-descretized version of the canonical variables.

A kinematical Hilbert space is constructed for the new theory with an SO(2) spin

network. In carry out quantization the new theory we follow a similar approach

from the kinematical Hilbert space. In addition, we provided the definition of the

physical scalar product (matrix element) of the projection operator. This matrix

element represents a sum over finite spin-foam amplitudes. As a result a very

trivial spinfoam is obtained as compared to the Ponzano-Regge spinfoam model.

This trivial spinfoam model has SO(2) spin networks as it boundaries. However in

{j1, j2, j3, j4, j5, j6} with the faces bounded by the vertex of a tetrahedron. This

new function is the Wigner 6j-symbol.

Appendix A

ADM Decomposition of 2 + 1

Gravity

The unification of space and time play a crucial role in general relativity. Physi-

cally, general relativity is the discovery that spacetime and gravitational field are

the same entity. What we call “spacetime” is itself a physical object in many

respects similar to the electromagnetic field. This led to the discovery that there

is no spacetime at all, and so what Newton called “space” and Minkowski called

“spacetime” is nothing but a dynamical object called the gravitational field [27].

The Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formalism however introduces an explicit- al-

though largely arbitrary division of spacetime into spatial and temporal divisions.

The decomposition of spacetime into space and time furnishes a natural setting

for the initial value problem, and it underlies Wheeler’s ’geometrodynamical’ pic-

ture of classical general relativity as the dynamics of evolving spatial geometries.

By providing a canonical description of the gravitational phase space, it leads

to a Hamiltonian version of classical gravity, and suggests a useful approach to

canonical quantization [5].

abstracts.value:
In this work, we review 3-dimensional gravity by canonically analyzing the HilbertPalatini action. We apply a time gauge used in 4-dimensional loop quantum gravity [14] to the simpler case of the 3-dimensional loop quantum gravity. By time
gauge fixing this Hilbert-Palatini action it leads to the Gauss constraints, the spatial diffeomorphism constraints, the Hamiltonian constraint and a new constraintC. The gauge symmetries generated by this new constraints are spacetime diffeomorphism and SO(2) gauge transformations. We solve the dynamics of the theory
by providing a regularization of the generalized projector operator in terms of the
Hamiltonian constraint. We provide the definition of the physical scalar product
which can be represented in terms of a sum over finite spinfoam amplitudes. Then
we establish a clear-cut link between the canonical quantization of the new theory
to the spinfoam model (Ponzano-Regge model) defined in terms of the SU (2) spin
networks.

titles.title: Time Gauge Fixing for 3d Loop Quantum Gravity

abstracts.value: Selecting an effective quantum compiler configuration requires coordinated decisions over both hardware targets and compiler settings, with the ultimate goal of improving circuit execution fidelity. Existing SOTA approaches typically decompose this problem into two sequential stages: a device is chosen first, after which compiler options are tuned on that device through RL-based search. This bottom-up strategy can be fundamentally limited by its initial device decision, since a poorly matched backend may constrain the best fidelity achievable regardless of how effectively later compiler options are optimized. In contrast to classical compiler tuning, where the search space is often prohibitively large, the configuration space of quantum compilers remains manageable enough to support exhaustive search. Consequently, rather than repeatedly searching from candidate configurations, one can derive reusable configuration knowledge from offline oracle results and apply it directly to new circuits. In this paper, we introduce a top-down configuration-selection paradigm and build QuOPTBench, an exhaustively searched benchmark containing oracle configurations for 268 quantum circuits. We first study whether LLMs can directly infer suitable configurations and evaluate ten representative LLMs. The results reveal that vanilla LLMs remain far from the oracle. We then employ an LLM to extract transferable rules from sampled circuits governing configuration selection. Using these rules together with predictors trained on the enumerated configuration data of the sampled circuits, we design QuTOP, a rule-guided ML framework that performs fast configuration selection without iterative online search. Across our evaluation, the distilled rules consistently strengthen LLM-based selection, while QuTOP provides the strongest overall balance between solution quality and selection latency among the baselines.

titles.title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm

abstracts.value: A quantum computer could recover the key of any Ethereum account whose public key appears on chain. We prove that no sidechain or bridge that leaves Ethereum's rules unchanged can protect such accounts: their funds must move into a contract whose release condition relies only on quantum-safe primitives. We design \emph{PQ-Vault}, a custody system for unmodified Ethereum combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain whose checkpoints carry compact certificates, and an optimistic dispute protocol. We give the first security proof of compact certificates against quantum attackers and a matching attack: with classically chosen parameters, the guarantee falls from 128 to about 60 bits, and a simple rule restores it. We show that a common seed-update rule in hash-chain proof of stake lets an attacker steer chosen slots and profit from splitting its stake, and give an election whose steering gain and inclusion delay are provably bounded against quantum attackers. Since compressing certificates with a pairing-based SNARK breaks quantum security, we use fraud proofs that need a single signature check. For 65,536 validators, a certificate is 0.8 MB, 260 times smaller than all signatures, and verifies in about 20 ms; the vault accepts a checkpoint for about 420,000 gas.

titles.title: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum

abstracts.value: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

titles.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?

abstracts.value: The same classical f-divergence admits inequivalent extensions to quantum states. The question is whether these extensions can be obtained from a common classical variational principle with an operational interpretation. Here we generalize Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization by introducing retrodictive tests relative to a reference state. A retrodictive test compares a forward and a reverse stochastic process, realized by quantum preparation and measurement, related by Petz transposition relative to the chosen reference, and subject to prescribed quantum averages. Equivalently, it compares two reverse tests sharing a reference output, whose labels are coupled by retrodiction. For faithful states in finite dimension, we prove that the same spectral implementation attains the minimum classical f-divergence over all admissible implementations simultaneously for every operator-convex f. A flat reference yields the standard quantum f-divergences, thereby giving the Nussbaum-Szkoła distributions a variational characterization. Choosing either prescribed state as reference recovers maximal quantum f-divergences and Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization, while power references interpolate between the standard and maximal divergences along the geodesic family. In the relative-entropy case, this gives the passage from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy by changing the reference state. The same optimization extends to arbitrary quantum channels and, for channels with faithful Choi operator, gives a variational characterization of quantum entropy production.

titles.title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodictive tests: a unifying classical variational principle

abstracts.value: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

titles.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace

abstracts.value: The Fröhlich-Pizzo (FP) model is a quantum-mechanical model originally developed to describe the interaction between an atom and the electromagnetic field in the nonrelativistic limit $c\to\infty$. We show that an adaptation of the FP model based on the local algebras of a $U(1)$ chiral current captures essential features of the horizon-induced decoherence mechanism identified by Danielson, Satishchandran, and Wald (DSW) in the limit of large holding time $T$. Our analysis suggests that the effective dynamics of the system undergoing decoherence in the DSW setting retains non-Markovian features. Our approach also offers a glimpse into the possible role of quantum events in the dynamics underlying horizon-induced decoherence.

titles.title: Adapted Fröhlich-Pizzo Model for Horizon-Induced Decoherence

abstracts.value: This work revisits the debate on fractional uncertainty relations that arose a decade ago and tries to settle it. After a careful study of the position-momentum uncertainty product of the Lévy wave packet, a novel lower bound is proposed for uncertainty relations in fractional quantum mechanics. This bound is nearly linear in the Lévy index and is satisfied by exact, calculable solutions available in the literature.

titles.title: The Lévy wave packet and fractional uncertainty relations

abstracts.value: When topological solitons are coupled to fermions, they often induce a nontrivial fermion number. In the chiral quark soliton model (CQSM), this phenomenon underlies the identification of soliton topology with baryon number. However, whether this topology--fermion-number correspondence is determined solely by soliton topology or also depends on the fermion--soliton coupling scheme remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate this question by comparing several coupling schemes to the same $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ chiral soliton background. To treat the corresponding Dirac Hamiltonians within a common framework, we evaluate the variation of the regularized fermion-number along a model-parameter space. For the standard chiral Yukawa coupling of the CQSM, this variation reproduces the topological charge $Q$ associated with $π_3(\mathrm{SU}(N))$. The same result is obtained for an axial-vector coupling, whereas the fermion number variation vanishes for a vector coupling, despite the nontrivial topology of the chiral soliton background. These results provide an explicit example in which soliton topology alone does not determine the fermionic response; the topology--fermion-number correspondence also depends on how the background field is coupled to fermions.

titles.title: Fermion-Number Variation for Several Coupling Schemes in an $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ Chiral Soliton Background

abstracts.value: We show that the concept of particles and antiparticles is related to the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$. Its generators are the position operators $\hat x^a$, the momentum operators $\hat p_a$, and the central element $Q_{\sf{v}}$, which defines a subgroup U(1)$_{\sf v}$ of $W\!H_3$. We show that the wave functions have a charge relative to the group U(1)$_{\sf{v}}$ equal to either $q_+=1/\hbar$ (particle $ψ_+$) or $q_-=-1/\hbar$ (antiparticle $ψ_-$). We call these eigenvalues of the operator $Q_{\sf{v}}$ quantum charges: $Q_{\sf{v}}ψ_\pm^{}=q_\pm^{}ψ_\pm^{}$. The wave functions $ψ_+$ and $ψ_-$ belong to the Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_+$ and $\mathcal{H}_-$, on which unitarily inequivalent representations $π_\hbar$ and $π_{-\hbar}$ of the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$ are defined. These representations are related to each other by the antilinear charge conjugation operator $\hat C$, which maps $\mathcal{H}_+, q_+$ to $\mathcal{H}_-, q_-$. Charges $q_\pm^{}$ are intrinsic characteristics of the wave functions $ψ_\pm^{}$, similar to spin and electric charge. The wave function possesses one of these charges, $q_+$ or $q_-$, prior to the specification of any equations. We show that negative probabilities/energies and the Klein paradox in Klein-Gordon and Dirac theories are consequences of the violation of U(1)$_{\sf v}$-invariance in these theories. Restoring this invariance separates particle and antiparticles and eliminates all paradoxes at the level of first-quantized relativistic theories.

titles.title: Quantum Charge as a Particle/Antiparticle Label

abstracts.value: Proton and neutron densities can have similar multipole moments while differing locally. We use differential forms to measure and locate such differences between nuclear mean fields. A pair invariant measures the angle between two density gradients, weighted by their magnitudes, and the coarea formula resolves its contribution over level surfaces. A triple invariant factorizes exactly into a weighted pair term and a directional term that measures the variation of a third field along the level-surface intersections. We test these quantities in 98 magnetized Wigner-Seitz solutions, five static Hartree-Fock configurations, an illustrative $^{16}$O + $^{34}$Mg collision, and periodic nuclear pasta (a slab and a connected network). The pair invariant distinguishes cell solutions with comparable proton quadrupole moments and is 253 times larger in $^{34}$Mg than in $^{24}$Mg; refinement to 0.6 fm changes it by at most 1.3% in the four configurations recomputed. The directional factor separates the sampled triaxial configurations from the prolate ones. In the collision, it accounts for the 7.3-fold rise of the triple before the first recorded low-density connection, while the weighted pair term changes by at most 3%. In nuclear pasta, slab and network configurations have similar integrated proton-neutron misalignment but different distributions over density levels; their triple invariants differ by a factor of about 370 on the finer grid, mainly due to the variation of the Coulomb potential along joint density levels. These comparisons require no preferred origin or axis. A resolved nonzero triple excludes a common symmetry axis, but zero does not establish one. The pasta results require further convergence studies.

titles.title: Relative geometry of nuclear mean fields through differential forms

abstracts.value: We establish that transversal diagonal gates on exact qubit codes of distance at least two can be exhaustively classified within a finite search space. Although code-preserving physical gates can have continuous phases, any projective logical action induced by a transversal diagonal gate can always be realized by a physical gate of finite order. Crucially, we prove that this physical order has an upper bound determined solely by the code parameters. This order bound enables the subset-sum-linear-programming (SSLP) framework introduced in arXiv:2504.20847 to exhaustively enumerate all candidate discrete symmetries, after which the Knill-Laflamme equations determine the remaining continuous code parameters. Applying this method to the nontrivial diagonal sector of exact $((6,2,3))$ codes, SSLP yields $66$ candidate symmetry classes, of which exactly $15$ are realizable, supporting full projective diagonal logical cyclic groups of orders $2$, $3$, and $5$. In particular, for order $5$, the code is unique up to local unitaries and qubit permutations, equivalent to the code constructed in arXiv:2504.20847. This code also attains the minimum length $n=6$ among exact $((n, 2, \ge 3))$ codes whose full projective transversal group cannot be conjugated into the projective Clifford group.

titles.title: Finite Classification of Transversal Diagonal Gates Beyond Stabilizer Codes

abstracts.value: The AnyonWiki is an open-source project that provides full algebraic and numerical data of fusion and unitary modular fusion categories as a resource for the scientific community. It comes with a database, the AnyonWikiDatabase, that currently includes the classification of multiplicity-free pivotal (braided) fusion categories through rank 7 and more than 25000 fusion rings including the classification of multiplicity-free fusion rings through rank 10, with work in progress to expand. This data is available through AnyonWiki.org, a website that provides robust search and download functionality and presents each fusion ring and category via a dedicated webpage. In this short article we discuss the data available at AnyonWiki.org as well as the scientific and communal motivations for the design of its underlying AnyonWikiDatabase, which are centered around making the data accessible, independently verifiable, granularly citable, useful, and easy to work with.

abstracts.value: We develop a generalized coordinate Bethe-ansatz framework for the massive Thirring model with an explicitly time-dependent fermion mass. Unlike the generalized Bethe ansatz for chiral quantum field theories, where particle transport acts in internal spin spaces and leads to quantum Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equations, the present construction acts directly on particle coordinates and physical rapidities. Its central new feature is a rapidity lattice. Because the time-dependent mass couples right- and left-moving components already in the one-particle sector, a fixed-rapidity block is not closed under spatial winding. Periodicity therefore requires all sectors generated by the finite shift $β\toβ-p$. Particle exchange relates amplitudes on this lattice through scalar analytic difference equations of Ruijsenaars type, whose solutions determine the complete time-dependent many-body wavefunction. Consistency of the coordinate construction also selects an exponential evolution of the bare mass, providing a new realization of the time dependent integrability-renormalization group correspondence. In the static limit, the rapidity-lattice construction reduces to the conventional massive-Thirring Bethe equations. Through the massive-Thirring/sine Gordon equivalence, the result also connects this exact quantum construction to the generalized space-time dependent Lax formalism.

titles.title: Generalized Coordinate Bethe Ansatz and Quantum Integrability of the Time-Dependent Massive Thirring Model

abstracts.value: We study the effects of massive Kaluza--Klein modes on the two-dimensional low-energy effective theory obtained by the $S^2$ reduction of four-dimensional Einstein--Maxwell theory on a Reissner--Nordström black hole background. We retain the first excited ($l=1$) Maxwell Kaluza--Klein modes in addition to the massless sector. The background electric flux mixes the Maxwell Kaluza--Klein scalars with the graviphotons, and tree-level exchange of the massive scalars generates a correction to the graviphoton kinetic term proportional to the square of the black hole charge. Within the leading local approximation, we also perturbatively evaluate the one-loop correction to the graviphoton kinetic term and find no dependence on the black hole charge. We find that near extremality, the charge-dependent tree-level correction becomes parametrically comparable to the classical graviphoton kinetic term.

titles.title: Graviphoton mixing with KK modes in the 2D effective theory of charged black holes

abstracts.value: We propose an extended local infrared cutoff for the holographic density that leads to linear cosmological equations and gives exact analytical solutions. The model allows to remove the residual matter and radiation-like terms of the local construction based on $H$ and $\dot{H}$, resulting in a clear separation between the standard cosmological fluids and the holographic sector. The homogeneous solution generates characteristic modes that give rise to different cosmological behaviors. The extension includes derivatives up to third order, where two of the characteristic modes can modify the pre-recombination expansion and reduce the sound horizon while remaining subdominant at BBN. A slightly phantom mode provides an additional late-time geometrical freedom that can further increase the CMB-compatible value of $H_0$. Optimizations using BAO constraints yield values of $H_0$ in the approximate range $70.5-72.4\ {\rm km\;s^{-1}\;Mpc^{-1}}$.

titles.title: Extended Local Infrared Cutoff for the Holographic Density

abstracts.value: We present an updated High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) analysis of the crowded Galactic-plane area near PSR J1928+1746, which was previously linked to the extended source 3HWC J1928+178. With 2904 days of HAWC data, improved event reconstruction, and a multicomponent likelihood model that includes six TeV source components and Galactic diffuse emission, we describe the region using six components and find a distinct, moderately extended source close to PSR J1928+1746. This source, HAWC J1928+1750, is detected from about 2 TeV to above 100 TeV and is well-described by a log-parabola spectrum with normalization $K = 5.0 \times 10^{-15}$ TeV$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at 12 TeV, index $α= 2.09$, curvature $β= 0.35$, and Gaussian extension $σ= 0.19^\circ$. Interpreting the emission using diffusion-halo templates under the assumption $B = 8 μ\mathrm{G}$ yields the diffusion coefficient D(100 TeV) = $2.1 \times 10^{27}$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$, which is about 500 times smaller than typical interstellar diffusion values at similar energies. This suggests that particle transport around PSR J1928+1746 is strongly suppressed under the TeV-halo interpretation. The TeV spectrum is consistent with leptonic inverse-Compton emission originating from pulsar-injected electrons and positrons, which requires less than approximately 1% of the pulsar's characteristic spin-down energy. However, a hadronic contribution from the surrounding environment cannot be excluded.

titles.title: Investigating a TeV-Halo Candidate around PSR J1928+1746 with HAWC

abstracts.value: We consider electric flux tube solutions in SU(3) gauge theory with scalar fields in the fundamental representation, for an electric field in the $λ_8$ direction (8-type). In temporal gauge, the 3-type electric field rotates within a single SU(2) subgroup at one frequency, whereas the 8-type electric field necessarily rotates within three SU(2) subgroups with at least two different frequencies. We construct the homogeneous 8-type electric field with three scalar fields and show that two scalar fields are sufficient only on a one-parameter family of gauge field backgrounds. Like the 3-type field, the homogeneous 8-type field is immune to decay through Schwinger pair production of gauge bosons. We then construct an 8-type electric string solution in temporal gauge. Its electric field is of 8-type on the string axis and, unlike the 3-type string, the string is only net color neutral, which results in a weak radial electric field.

titles.title: 8-type electric flux tube solutions in SU(3) gauge theory

abstracts.value: Quantum Multi-Programming (QMP) enables the simultaneous execution of quantum circuits from multiple users on a single quantum chip in cloud quantum computing services. However, QMP is vulnerable to crosstalk attacks, in which a malicious user deliberately induces crosstalk to disrupt other users' computations. As a countermeasure, prior work has proposed the use of buffer qubits, which remain idle and are allocated between quantum circuits to suppress the effect of crosstalk. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, such countermeasures have not been publicly reported in production quantum cloud software. In this paper, we extend the QMP of OQTOPUS, open-source software that is already in production use for operating real quantum computers, with a buffer-qubit-based circuit allocation method. Experiments on a real device characterize the attack effect in terms of energy relaxation and dephasing, showing that observable degradation appears in dephasing characteristics of qubits adjacent to the attacker circuit. Based on this result, we release the proposed method as part of OQTOPUS and confirm that the buffer qubits are correctly reserved around the allocated circuits.

titles.title: Buffer-Qubit-Based Quantum Circuit Allocation Method Against Crosstalk Attacks

abstracts.value: Based on the oscillation modes of a bunch subject to the space-charge force, we discuss the decoherence of the dipole oscillation, the beam transfer function, and the beam instability. The longitudinal phase space is discretized into \(n_l\times n_J\) grids in the azimuthal and radial directions, respectively. The transverse dipole moment in the longitudinal phase space is represented by a vector of length \(n_l n_J\), and the transformation given by the Vlasov equation is represented by a matrix transformation of size \(n_l n_J\times n_l n_J\). Solving the eigenvalue problem of this matrix gives the \(n_l n_J\) eigen-oscillation modes of the bunch. Using the resulting eigenvectors within a standard linear-algebraic treatment, we analyze these three phenomena. The analysis was performed for the Rapid Cycling Synchrotron (RCS) of the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) using \(n_l=41\) and \(n_J=40\), and it visualizes the features related to the continuous distribution of the tune, Landau damping, and isolated modes separated from the continuous tune region.

titles.title: Oscillation modes, Decoherence, Beam Transfer Functions, and Instabilities for a Beam Subjected to Space-Charge Forces

abstracts.value: Distance integration can conceal the spatial organization of neutron pairing in a reflection-asymmetric intrinsic configuration. We resolve the spin-singlet pairing tensor by relative distance and signed pair-center position along a prescribed $α$+$^{42}$Ca-like path in $^{46}$Ti, using density-constrained Skyrme Hartree--Fock plus Bardeen--Cooper--Schrieffer calculations. Compact and extended components have oppositely signed shifts relative to the normal-density product conditioned on the same distance interval. At a reference center separation of 6 fm, the distance-integrated difference is 0.010, whereas the compact--extended contrast is 0.439. For the baseline surface-pairing prescription, this contrast increases between reference center separations of 6 and 7 fm while the extended anomalous weight decreases and the average neutron gap increases. Endpoint partitions locate an excess of extended neutron weight with both nucleons on the core side. An interference-retaining analysis in the stored canonical representation links the anomalous redistribution to $f_{7/2}$-weighted branches gaining core-side support with distinct amplitude responses. Changes in the normal-density reference contribute separately to the growing contrast. The conditional neutron pattern persists under the tested functional and pairing variations. Distance-conditioned distributions thus reveal intrinsic pairing structure hidden by scalar measures and distance integration.

titles.title: Spatial asymmetry of neutron pairing:A distance-resolved study of $^{46}\mathrm{Ti}$

abstracts.value: The effective field theory (EFT) of contact forces which describes few-nucleon systems at distance scales larger than the pion Compton wavelength ${\rm EFT}({π\hskip-0.54em /})$ can be defined in terms of momentum-dependent potentials that contain a fixed number of simple poles and generate the effective-range expansion to a given fixed order. These potentials provide a practical generalization of the standard ${\rm EFT}({π\hskip-0.54em /})$ power-counting scheme which, for instance, naturally accounts for the large effective ranges in the s-wave channels. Nucleon-nucleon phase shifts computed in this formulation of ${\rm EFT}({π\hskip-0.54em /})$ are compared to modern phase-shift analyses, and effective-range parameters are tabulated. The ${\rm EFT}({π\hskip-0.54em /})$ potentials, which provide a rational approximation of the S-matrix, are easily extended into the regime of pion physics through the inclusion of additional S-matrix poles and zeros, and provide an accurate description of data up to pion-production threshold. The potentials in this scheme are in an important sense weak over all relevant distance scales, and are therefore of utility for systematic calculations of many-nucleon observables.

titles.title: Reformulation of the pionless effective field theory for practical few- and many-body applications

abstracts.value: Reaching a degenerate ground-state manifold and sampling it uniformly are distinct properties of a quantum annealer. We quantify this distinction using an Ising ring with additional couplings between maximally separated sites. For antiferromagnetic benchmark couplings and $N \geq 5$, we derive the exact ground-state energy, degeneracy, and defect structure for each congruence class of $N$ modulo four. This classification separates ground-state hit probability from conditional sampling bias. We embed instances with up to 162 logical spins on a D-Wave Advantage processor using length-two chains and compare its output with simulated annealing on the embedded and logical problems. For a frustrated $N=83$ instance, the processor visits 164 of the 166 exact ground states, yet the conditional distributions over states and defect sectors remain nonuniform. For $N=160$, the processor has a larger ground-state hit probability than logical simulated annealing (0.869 versus 0.519), but also a larger total-variation distance from uniformity (0.317 versus 0.136). A pause during the anneal raises the ground-state hit probability from 0.42 to 0.86 without restoring uniform sampling. These results identify a relaxation window and demonstrate that optimization success and sampling quality need not improve together, providing an exactly characterized benchmark for open-system quantum annealing.

titles.title: Optimization versus fair sampling in quantum annealing: An exactly characterized frustrated Ising benchmark

abstracts.value: Context. Photometric-redshift uncertainties redistribute galaxy pairs along the line of sight (LOS), diluting spatial clustering measurements. Propagating full redshift probability density functions (PDFs) through standard pair-count estimators remains computationally demanding. Aims. We present $ν$Gundam, a unified framework to propagate radial PDFs at the pair-count level while retaining a common interface for exact, compressed, and stochastic projected-clustering calculations. Methods. The code implements four modes: exact empirical-PDF integration, Gaussian-mixture compression, Monte Carlo (MC) sampling, and a quantile-compression method. All modes accumulate pair counts on a resolved ($r_\mathrm{p},π$) grid, from which $ξ(r_\mathrm{p},π)$ and $w_\mathrm{p}(r_\mathrm{p};Π)$ are reconstructed. We validate these with DESI galaxies and CosmoDC2 mocks. Results. The PDF-aware modes produce nearly indistinguishable LOS redistribution kernels, while point-photo-$z$ estimates discard probabilistic pair information. Radial uncertainty mainly redistributes the clustering signal to larger $π$; the depth required to recover the truth projection scales with the pairwise radial dispersion. For practical settings, MC, quantile, and Gaussian-mixture compression reproduce the exact result with fractional RMS residuals below 5%. Applied to DESI Bright Galaxy Survey samples, MC sampling recovers spectroscopic clustering shapes and relative amplitudes for $r_\mathrm{p}\gtrsim0.8\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ using sample-dependent recovery depths of ~400 and ~$180\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ for red and blue galaxies. Conclusions. Projected clustering with redshift PDFs is a pair-redistribution problem. When propagated consistently, the signal is recovered accurately and efficiently. The integration depth is sample dependent and should be part of the measurement definition rather than a fixed choice.

titles.title: $ν$Gundam: a unified framework for point-redshift and PDF-aware spatial correlation functions

abstracts.value: A circuit parameter can change measured features without changing their projected Gaussian kernel. We characterize this lost dependence and distinguish recovery by metric design from nonlinear feature expansion. With analytic feature coefficients, a fixed finite data basis affinely independent on the input domain, a fixed positive definite metric, and fixed bandwidth, the coefficient Gram matrix determines all-input kernel equivalence, global coordinate inactivity, and generic differential rank. An exact four-qubit family exhibits a sharp boundary: diagonal metrics give rank two, dense metrics reach but cannot exceed three, and no fixed affine expansion crosses this ceiling. One appended nonlinear scalar coordinate suffices for rank four and is minimal when the original features are retained. A single pairwise product achieves this with an explicit nondiagonal metric; a scalar sum of two products achieves it with a diagonal metric. Both use existing ideal local means. Exact certificates establish ranks in 54 selected circuit/readout settings. Matched finite-shot comparisons show that minimal representation size need not give the best sensitivity among the tested designs. Under a factorized measurement distribution, conditional product estimation cannot increase variance at a fixed design. Execution audits further separate kernel identifiability from compiled cost.

abstracts.value: Quantum circuit optimization is a key step toward the efficient execution of quantum algorithms. Template matching has emerged as one of the dominant approaches for simplifying quantum circuits, yet it confronts the intrinsic challenge of accommodating gate commutativity. The state-of-the-art template-matching algorithm relies on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation. While this DAG-based technique handles gate commutativity satisfactorily, it fails to preserve the local connectivity inherent to quantum circuits, thereby leading to relatively high matching complexity. In this paper, we introduce a hypergraph representation (HG), a commutativity-aware representation that collapses commuting gates into a single super-node while retaining all local connectivity. This enables matches to be extended locally without revisiting the rest of the circuit, with incremental updates limited to the immediate neighborhood. Experimental results demonstrate that our HG matcher achieves 11--606x speed-up over the DAG-based implementation in Qiskit (Iten et al., 2022) on both random and arithmetic benchmarks, while maintaining the same optimization quality. The acceleration increases with circuit size, confirming that preserving locality and connectivity is the key to scalable quantum circuit optimisation.

titles.title: Fast Template Matching for Quantum Circuits Using Hypergraph

abstracts.value: A ligand can adopt multiple conformations within the same binding site, and these conformations can interact differently with the surrounding protein. Multiconformer modeling must therefore determine which candidate conformations to retain and what occupancies to assign to them. An established automated approach uses mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) with hard occupancy and conformer-count limits for this selection. Here, we reformulated conformer selection as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem with finite penalties and discrete occupancies. We solved the QUBO using a quantum-classical hybrid solver. We compared this workflow with the MIQP-based qFit-ligand workflow across 83 paired X-ray ligand entries using the same experimental inputs and the same qFit-ligand processing protocol. For each entry, both final models were evaluated against the same composite-omit map generated from the common input structure before the two workflows diverged. Quantum-qFit produced higher ligand-region real-space correlation coefficients (RSCC) in 62 entries 74.7% and lower occupancy-weighted torsional strain in 66 entries 79.5%. Similar directional trends remained in the 28 entries with matched final conformer counts. The molecular Electron Density for Individual Atoms score (EDIAm) decreased in most entries. This result shows that higher regional map agreement did not necessarily correspond to stronger atom-level density support. Overall, the results show that the conformer-selection formulation can change which ligand states are represented from the same experimental data and provide a QUBO framework for studying multiconformer ligand selection.

titles.title: QUBO-Based Conformer Selection with Quantum-Classical Hybrid Optimization for Multiconformer Ligand Modeling

abstracts.value: We relate black-hole horizons and wormhole throats to the geometry of the harmonic branches of Einstein--Maxwell--dilaton gravity. In the unified Ernst framework, we first solve the harmonic equations prior to fixing the spatial harmonic, and then jointly reconstruct the metric, Maxwell four-potential, and scalar field. The conserved geodesic energy fixes the meridional Weyl quadrature, whereas the initial geodesic data capture the asymptotic charges. Choosing the Schwarzschild harmonic function, regular nonextremal horizons fix the normalization \(H=1\) along with the associated matter-field regularity requirements. This reproduces the Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom families (including the NUT extension), the Gibbons-Maeda solution, and the dyonic string and Kaluza--Klein solutions, while also preserving their more general branches. If the scalar sector is continued to the phantom sign, one obtains a complementary oblate construction: smooth continuation selects \(H=-1\) and produces the massive and ultrastatic Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes. By comparing with the vacuum ring geometry, we make clear the further importance of the global extension. Altogether, these findings offer a unified black-hole--wormhole geometric reading of the charge relations and regularity constraints for the reconstructed solutions.

titles.title: Harmonic branches of Einstein--Maxwell--scalar field gravity: exact solutions and regularity

abstracts.value: The r-modes in rotating neutron stars are a promising source of continuous gravitational waves, and may grow or be excited to amplitudes $α\lesssim1$. We perform general relativistic simulations of nonlinear $l=|m|=2$ r-modes in a rapidly rotating neutron star with spin frequency $f_{spin}\approx792$ Hz, relaxing the Cowling and small-$α$ approximations. The star is idealised as an unmagnetised, one-component, perfect fluid with a polytropic equation of state. The r-mode frequency is measured to be $f_{r-mode}=1014$ Hz for initial amplitude $α_0=0.2$. The dimensionless frequency $κ\approx0.7197$ agrees with an estimate from linear perturbation theory to within 1.7%. $f_{r-mode}$ increases quadratically with amplitude, and $κ$ decreases by 3.4% across simulations where $α_0$ is varied through the range $0.2\leqα_0\leq1.2$. The gravitational wave strain calculated from the Newman-Penrose scalar implies $h_{r-mode}\approx9.7\times10^{-22}$ at $10$ kpc for $α_0=0.2$, which agrees with Einstein's quadrupole formula to within 35%. We also report on nonlinear phenomena observed in our simulations, e.g. differential rotation, amplitude decay, and signatures of nonlinear mode coupling in the spacetime oscillations.

titles.title: General Relativistic Simulations of the Nonlinear Evolution of r-modes in Rapidly Rotating Neutron Stars

abstracts.value: The EMPRESS collaboration has reported a primordial helium mass fraction \(Y_P = 0.2402 \pm 0.0040\), which lies more than \(1σ\) below the standard Big Bang Nucleosynthesis prediction. Combined with the deuterium abundance and the Planck baryon density, this corresponds to a mild \(\sim 2σ\) tension with the standard value of the effective number of relativistic species, or to a \(\sim 2σ\) indication of a non-zero electron-neutrino degeneracy. We show that it can be explained by non-unitary three-neutrino mixing, a generic feature of seesaw extensions of the Standard Model. Non-unitarity makes the Fermi constant in beta decay exceed that in muon decay, enhancing the neutron-to-proton conversion rate and lowering \(Y_P\). A full numerical BBN calculation, combined with the EMPRESS \(Y_P\) determination and the deuterium abundance gives the best fit point at \(α_{22}=0.982\), while the standard values \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=3.044\), \(ξ_e=0\) remain allowed; the required level of non-unitarity is consistent with current experimental constraints.

titles.title: Low Primordial Helium as a Probe of Non-Unitary Neutrino Mixing

abstracts.value: We investigate a formulation of the Standard Model in which gauge and Higgs fields are regulated on a finite lattice, while quarks and leptons remain continuum Weyl fermions. This preserves the familiar continuum description of anomalies, spectral flow, and fermion zero modes, without requiring a finite-dimensional discretization of chiral fermions. The Standard Model's anomaly cancellation permits a gauge-invariant definition of the chiral fermion determinant. Yukawa interactions are included in the full fermion determinant using a gauge-covariant cutoff that acts on the interaction vertices rather than the fermion propagator. We show that removing this cutoff requires only the local subtractions expected from one-loop power counting, and construct a consistent complex fermion weight, including in topologically nontrivial backgrounds. At fixed bosonic lattice spacing and finite spacetime volume, the resulting bosonic functional integral is finite and exactly gauge invariant under the stated smoothness conditions. The construction provides a finite-regulator Standard Model formulation retaining the physical structure of continuum chiral fermions. Appendix F.5 establishes reflection positivity for a variant reconstruction at zero Yukawa coupling and zero theta. The bosonic continuum limit remains open.

titles.title: The Standard Model on a finite bosonic lattice with continuum Weyl fermions

abstracts.value: We study static, spherically symmetric wormholes in deRham--Gabadadze--Tolley massive gravity with the spatially degenerate Vegh reference metric. The effective fluid carried by the massive graviton contributes nothing to the combination of density and radial pressure that the flare-out condition constrains, so it is invisible to the null energy condition along radial light rays. This holds for the whole degenerate class of reference metrics, for all four interaction potentials, and for any static spherically symmetric geometry; the same property singles out the Vegh choice as the only consistent one. The matter alone must therefore violate the null energy condition at every throat, exactly as in general relativity. This corrects a claim repeated across the massive-gravity wormhole literature. We then determine where throats may sit. Wormholes with isotropic pressure fall into two families. One lies beyond the cosmological horizon of the theory's own vacuum and has no static exterior; it is empty in general relativity and is switched on by the graviton coupling. The other lies inside that horizon and needs a steeply falling redshift. We give exact perfect-fluid solutions for both. In the second family the graviton term can turn the tension at the throat into ordinary pressure. A thin shell closes the configuration, and its surface stresses and its exotic-matter content follow in closed form. The shells are radially unstable, and light rays near the throat trace an unstable circular orbit.

titles.title: Wormholes in Vegh--dRGT massive gravity: a null-energy transparency theorem, horizon obstruction, and exact isotropic solutions

abstracts.value: Encounters of stellar-mass black holes (sBH) in active galactic nuclei discs naturally form mean-motion resonances of sBH pairs. These mean-motion resonances can be broken close to the central supermassive black hole when gravitational-wave emission dominates over gas torques. We derive a simple condition that depends only on the sBH mass ratio and the resonance index for which a pair of sBH in a mean-motion resonance will remain intact and can be detectable as a multiple Extreme-Mass-Ratio-Inspirals (mEMRIs) in the LISA band. We present for the first time the gravitational-wave strain signatures of a pair of co-migrating sBH in mean-motion resonance, including additional gravitational-wave harmonics associated with orbital conjunctions of the individual EMRIs. The frequency evolution and the associated chirp mass is degenerate with isolated EMRIs of different masses. However, the mEMRI mass ratio is quantised by the resonance order and is larger than the true mass ratio. The degeneracy can be broken if the true sBH mass ratio can be inferred from individual strain amplitudes. We argue that mEMRIs should be common if disc driven EMRIs are to be detected by LISA, with $\sim 10$ mEMRIs per year in the local universe ($z \lesssim 0.2$), highlighting the need to model mEMRI systems in future LISA data analysis.

titles.title: Lasting mEMRIs: Signatures of Multiple Black Hole Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals from AGN discs

abstracts.value: We derive sufficient criteria that guarantee convergence of open quantum system dynamics to a unique long-time state independent of the initial conditions. We refer to this behavior as complete relaxation. Focusing on systems described by Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equations on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, our approach uses only elementary mathematical arguments. For autonomous systems, we recover three previously derived relaxation criteria, which can be expressed as algebraic conditions on the Lindblad operators and the Hamiltonian entering the GKSL equation. For periodically driven systems, we obtain a new criterion involving a similar algebraic condition and a local continuity requirement on the time-dependent GKSL generator. This result implies an earlier criterion for complete relaxation formulated in Ref. [J. Phys. A 52, 43LT01 (2019)]. We also discuss implications of our approach for periodically modulated classical master equations, as well as extensions to driven systems without a periodicity constraint.

titles.title: Algebraic criteria for complete relaxation in autonomous and periodically driven open quantum systems

abstracts.value: Within nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) factorization, we calculate the next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections to $χ_{bJ}\to J/ψ+γ$ with $J=0,1,2$. We determine all six independent helicity amplitudes, including the one-loop corrections to the QED amplitude and the two-loop corrections to the QCD amplitude, and retain the interference between the QED and QCD amplitudes in the decay widths. The NLO corrections substantially enhance the $χ_{b0}$ and $χ_{b1}$ decay widths, while reducing the $χ_{b2}$ decay width by approximately $36\%$. Including the QED amplitude leads to sizable destructive interference for $χ_{b0}$ and an enhancement for $χ_{b2}$, but has only a small effect on the $χ_{b1}$ decay width. Two treatments of photon fragmentation, based on the NRQCD matrix element and the experimentally determined $J/ψ$ decay constant, yield NLO unpolarized decay widths that agree at the few percent level or better. Using the decay constant scheme at $μ_R=m_b$, we obtain NLO central branching fractions of $1.03\times10^{-6}$, $1.45\times10^{-5}$, and $1.99\times10^{-6}$ for the three channels, respectively. The NLO corrections reduce the renormalization scale dependence, particularly for $χ_{b2}$, although a sizable dependence remains for $χ_{b0}$. At fixed $m_b$, the branching fractions decrease with increasing $r=m_c/m_b$, more strongly for $χ_{b1}$ and $χ_{b2}$ than for $χ_{b0}$. For $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=14\,{\rm TeV}$ and an integrated luminosity of $100\,{\rm fb}^{-1}$, we estimate about $1.9\times10^4$ and $4.8\times10^4$$\ell^+\ell^-γ$ events from $χ_{b0}$ and $χ_{b2}$ decays, respectively. Measurements with the existing Belle $Υ(2S)$ sample remain challenging because of the small expected yields. A larger $Υ(2S)$ sample at Belle II would improve the prospects for observing these radiative decays.

titles.title: Next-to-leading-order QCD corrections to the radiative decays $χ_{bJ}\to J/ψ+γ$

abstracts.value: We report a rapid optical changing-look event in the Seyfert galaxy NGC 3227: the optical continuum faded by more than 70% and broad H-beta emission nearly disappeared within weeks, before recovering within two months. Damped random walk simulations calibrated to the source's normal variability show that such a decline is unlikely for stochastic accretion fluctuations (p = 0.002). Simultaneous Swift monitoring reveals X-ray spectral hardening, pointing to enhanced line-of-sight absorption. During the dim state, reverberation mapping yields a persistent 6-8 day lag between the continuum and broad H-beta, showing that the broad-line region continued to reverberate and placing the obscurer interior to the broad-line region. Photoionization calculations require a fully ionized, Compton-thick column with N_H ~ 1.5 x 10^24 cm^-2 to reproduce the optical continuum suppression. Together, these observations demonstrate that compact, high-column-density obscurers interior to the broad-line region can produce extreme optical changing-look behavior on week timescales.

titles.title: NGC 3227 Blinks: An Extreme Changing-Look Event in a Seyfert Galaxy

abstracts.value: We investigate weak lensing effects of a chiral gravitational wave background (GWB) as a new mechanism for generating parity-odd correlations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Accounting for both photon deflection and polarization rotation, we derive the resulting parity-odd EB and TB angular power spectra. For representative GWB energy density spectra, we find parameter choices that provide good fits to existing measurements. This mechanism provides a potential observational probe of chiral GWB, which can arise in a wide range of theoretical scenarios.
